title: Dry summers gave no clear extra October-March rainfall in England and Wales for 1836-2024
abstract: We tested whether dry June-August periods were followed by extra October-March rain in England and Wales. We used Met Office country rainfall records for 189 summer years from 1836 to 2024. After linear trend removal, the mean country partial correlation was 0.043. Its 95% paired five-year block interval was -0.080 to 0.172. Negative correlation would support compensation. For the driest fifth of summers, the following-season rainfall contrast against other years was +7.2 mm in England and -10.4 mm in Wales. Both intervals included zero. Shorter-period and seasonal-window checks also left the main link uncertain. These records do not show clear automatic rainfall compensation after dry summers. They do not prove independence or measure recovery of water stores. Country averages, revised data, linear trend removal and block assumptions limit inference. We supply monthly inputs, source hashes, seasonal pairs, code, draws, a figure and a numerical audit.

display.caption: Seasonal rainfall residuals and mean country partial correlations. Lines show 95% paired five-year block intervals. Negative correlations indicate compensation.

citations.reason: River-flow drought termination gives the context. We test a rainfall precursor, not flow recovery.
